From a large kettle. See Mishnah Berurah for the reason, and see Pri Megadim, who writes that this concern applies only when the kettle is still somewhat lukewarm because it was removed from the fire only a short time earlier. If it cooled for a long time, there is plainly no concern.

And the water in it is lukewarm. If it cooled completely, everyone permits it, even according to those who are stringent regarding water that had been heated by fire and then cooled, because here it was not originally fire-heated water, as stated in seif katan 29. [Later authorities]

One may rely on them. Bach is stringent in every case, but several later authorities rule like the Shulchan Aruch and Rama. Even according to Bach, if the water was drawn from rivers, one may rely upon the lenient view after the fact when the mistake was inadvertent, because according to Rashi the essential law of mayim shelanu applies specifically to spring water. Likewise, if mayim shelanu became hot and was cooled and dough was kneaded with it inadvertently, there is room for leniency even according to Bach. Eliyah Rabbah writes likewise.

Water that did not remain overnight and was nullified 1 in 2, etc. If hot or lukewarm water became mixed with a large quantity of cold water until it cooled, Olat Shabbos, Chok Yaakov, and Eliyah Rabbah, as also cited by Shulchan Aruch HaRav, are lenient because it became nullified in the cold water. Chok Yosef and Bigdei Yesha are stringent, and Magen HaElef likewise implies stringency. Pri Megadim also questions the leniency, because we find it stated only regarding mayim shelanu. Therefore, initially one must certainly be careful not to knead with such water. After the fact, however, where there is a major financial loss or the loss of Yom Tov rejoicing, one may be lenient. Bigdei Yesha writes likewise.

1) [Seif 1] When he awakens from his sleep, etc. How good and pleasant it is if a person is able to refrain from speaking anything at all, so that the first words he speaks upon rising from sleep begin with a mitzvah, blessing the Creator of his soul. This is very proper. Chesed LaAlafim, letter 2. See Moreh BeEtzba, letter 63, and what we wrote above in siman 1, letter 40.

2) Tur writes that after putting on tefillin one should arrange the blessings, etc. We already wrote above in siman 25, letter 26, that the Arizal would recite all the morning blessings through the passage of the Akeidah, and afterward wrap himself in a tallis, put on tefillin, and pray.

3) There, upon awakening he should say Elokai Neshamah. This blessing does not begin with Baruch because it is a blessing of thanksgiving, and blessings of thanksgiving do not begin with Baruch, as Maran writes in siman 6, seif 3. Nevertheless, it should be placed adjacent to Asher Yatzar, as we wrote above in siman 6, letters 3 and 5, in the name of the Arizal. See also below, letter 7.

4) There, he should say Elokai Neshamah. One should pause slightly between Elokai and neshamah, so that it not sound as though the soul is his god, Heaven forbid. Abudraham; Ateret Zekenim; Eliyah Rabbah, letter 1; Shaliach Tzibbur, page 45d; Beit Oved, letter 1; Chesed LaAlafim, letter 3; Yafeh LaLev, letter 2; Ben Ish Chai, Parashat Vayeshev, letter 2.

5) One should not say "tehorah hi," but simply "tehorah, Atah beratah," because in most cases a person has sinned and the soul is not literally pure. Kesher Gudal, siman 5, letter 8. Shaliach Tzibbur, page 46a, gives additional reasons. Beit Oved, letter 2; Chesed LaAlafim; Ben Ish Chai there. See Yafeh LaLev, letter 4, who discusses this at length. In Berachot 60b the word hi is also absent. Although Shaar HaKavanos, page 2a, has "tehorah hi," this need not be exact, and the custom is not to say hi.

6) There, he should say Elokai Neshamah. This blessing should contain 47 words, corresponding to the combined numerical values of Havayah and Ehyeh, which represent Abba and Imma that are never separated. See Nahar Shalom, page 11c in the newer edition, and what we wrote above in siman 6, letter 3. Shaliach Tzibbur and Chesed LaAlafim write likewise.

The text is: "My God, the soul You placed within me is pure. You created it; You formed it; You breathed it into me; and You preserve it within me. You will ultimately take it from me and restore it to me in the future. As long as the soul is within me, I give thanks before You, Hashem my God and God of my fathers, Master of all works, Lord of all souls. Blessed are You, Hashem, Who restores souls to dead bodies." Chesed LaAlafim. This is unlike Ateret Zekenim in siman 6 and Beit Oved following him, who omit the word "bi" after "You breathed it." Shaliach Tzibbur rejects their view and writes that the universal custom, as well as the Gemara in Berachot 60b and Shaar HaKavanos, includes it.

8) There, he should say Elokai Neshamah. If he mistakenly recited Mechayeh HaMeitim instead of Elokai Neshamah, he has fulfilled his obligation. Peri Chadash; Yad Aharon; Kesher Gudal, siman 5, letter 9; Shaliach Tzibbur, page 46b; Beit Oved in the laws of Birchot HaShachar; Shitilei Zeitim, letter 1. Although Maamar Mordechai questions Peri Chadash, he ultimately writes that his view must be taken into account, and the rule of doubt regarding blessings supports leniency.

9) If one forgot Birchot HaShachar before prayer, he should recite them afterward, except for HaMachazir Neshamot, because Mechayeh HaMeitim has already exempted him, and except for Birchot HaTorah, because Ahavat Olam has already exempted him. This will be explained below in siman 47, seifim 7 and 8, and in Rama at the end of siman 52. If he failed to recite them even after prayer, see below, siman 71, letter 4, regarding how long their time continues. Initially, however, it is obvious that one should not postpone Birchot HaShachar until after prayer, because doing so reverses the order of the spiritual rectifications they effect. See Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaBerachot, chapter 3, and Nahar Shalom, page 11c in the newer edition.

7) There, he should say Elokai Neshamah. The blessing "Elokai, the soul You placed within me," etc., is adjacent to the preceding blessing because it corresponds to Imma, which is always joined with Abba. Understand this. Although not every person merits the specific soul-level called neshamah, every person nevertheless possesses a portion in the soul of Adam HaRishon, which included all created souls, even if this individual has not yet personally merited that level.

The phrase "it is pure" corresponds to Atzilut, from which comes the neshamah of the neshamah. "You created it" corresponds to the part of the neshamah that comes from Beriah. "You formed it" alludes to ruach, which comes from Yetzirah. "You breathed it into me" alludes to nefesh, which is in Asiyah. Thus, by saying "the soul You placed within me," he includes all 4 of these aspects and calls them collectively neshamah.

"You will ultimately take it from me," etc., alludes to the mystical elevation of mayin nukvin. Malchut receives the souls of the righteous in the secret of "new every morning" so that they become mayin nukvin within it; afterward, "You will ultimately restore it to me" in the morning, likewise in the secret of "new every morning." Shaar HaKavanos, page 2a. See the discourses concerning the night, discourse 3, page 53, and understand. See Shaliach Tzibbur, pages 45d and 46a, who explains the matter differently. Beit Oved, Chesed LaAlafim, and other siddurim write that while saying Elokai Neshamah one should intend an interweaving of the letters of neshamah with the letters of his own name. See Yafeh LaLev, letter 3. Since the Arizal did not write this and our practice does not follow it, we have not recorded it further.

(17) "A person fulfills his obligation," etc. This is after the fact. For an elderly or ill person who finds it difficult to eat dry matzah, it is permitted even initially to soak the matzah in water. One must, however, take care that it not remain soaked for 24 hours, because something soaked for 24 hours is treated as cooked.

(18) "Soaked." Meaning soaked in water. Whether it may be soaked in other beverages, fruit juice, or soup is disputed by the halachic authorities. Some prohibit it because those liquids weaken the taste of the matzah by imparting their own flavor. Others hold that only cooking removes the taste of matzah, but soaking does not. Therefore, an elderly or ill person who cannot eat matzah soaked in water may soak it in wine or another beverage. An ordinary person, however, who ate matzah soaked in a liquid other than water has not fulfilled his obligation and must eat another matzah, both for the kezayit over which the matzah blessing is recited and for the kezayit of afikoman.

(19) "Provided it did not dissolve." If the matzah dissolved to the point that it lost the form of bread, one does not fulfill the obligation with it. If it merely softened but its substance and appearance remain recognizable, it is valid.

(20) "As long as the flavor of matzah remains." Even if the water is warm, it is valid provided it is not so hot as to constitute actual cooking. If the water reached a temperature at which ordinary contact cannot be comfortably maintained, there is concern that the matzah has been cooked and one does not fulfill the obligation with it. The same applies all the more when it was placed in a kli rishon.
